queue_items.claim: The strongest_rejected_alternative rejects the internal split at web:Ps.19.10|Ps.19.11 solely on divine-name texture -- 'one panel whose sevenfold Yahweh count marks it as one unit' -- which sec.2f bars as a boundary driver by itself, and the count's own distribution does not support the unifying inference.
queue_items.grounds: Ps strategy sec.2f: divine-name texture is 'TEXTURE ONLY -- never a boundary driver by itself'. Byte distribution across the panel: 6 of the 7 tokens stand at MT 19:8-10 (= web:Ps.19.7-Ps.19.9) and the seventh at MT 19:15 (= web:Ps.19.14); MT 19:11 and MT 19:12 (= web:Ps.19.10 and web:Ps.19.11), the two verses the rival would split between, carry no divine-name token at all -- the row's own oss[1] states exactly this for web:Ps.19.11-Ps.19.13. The count is therefore silent at the proposed seam and cannot be what marks the panel as one unit. The row's front seam is unaffected (it rests on the addressee shift shared with M8-Ps-045) and its back edge is the psalm's end, so the defect is confined to the rival's stated rejection ground.
queue_items.proposed_change: Field repair (strongest_rejected_alternative): re-ground the rejection on a ruled tier-1 signal -- one unbroken addressee and the law-catalogue-to-response movement running through web:Ps.19.7-Ps.19.14 with no speaker or addressee change at web:Ps.19.10|Ps.19.11 -- and demote the sevenfold count to corroboration. No span change; routes onward for adjudication.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: “Yahweh's law is perfect, restoring the soul” (web:Ps.19.7) opens the torah-panel by naming the covenant name יְהוָ֣ה, Yahweh (oshb:Ps.19.8), which recurs seven times across four verses in this panel — web:Ps.19.7, Ps.19.8, Ps.19.9, and Ps.19.14 (sweep: 7 occurrences across 4 verses, confirmed by sweep.py --skel's verse hits and the whole-psalm inventory's yhwh:7 total) — against the one אֵ֑ל token of the panel before it (oshb:Ps.19.2). Three verses of synonym-paired praise for the law (law/covenant at web:Ps.19.7, precepts/commandment at web:Ps.19.8, fear/ordinances at web:Ps.19.9) run through “sweeter also than honey and the extract of the honeycomb” (web:Ps.19.10) before “Moreover your servant is warned by them” (web:Ps.19.11) turns from describing the law's qualities to the psalmist's own response, closing on the prayer formula “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, Yahweh, my rock, and my redeemer” (web:Ps.19.14), which readdresses Yahweh directly and closes the psalm.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this panel at web:Ps.19.10-Ps.19.11 into separate law-description and response strophes would divide one panel whose sevenfold Yahweh count marks it as one unit against the heavens panel, not evidence for a finer-grained seam within it.
observed_substrate_signals: יְהוָ֣ה (Yahweh) occurs twice each at oshb:Ps.19.8, oshb:Ps.19.9, oshb:Ps.19.10 and once at oshb:Ps.19.15 — seven token-occurrences across four verses (sweep: 7 occurrences across 4 verses)
no divine-name token (Yahweh or El) appears at web:Ps.19.11-Ps.19.13, the personal-response verses between the law's praise and the closing prayer formula
shipped_row.device_notes: No selah interrupts web:Ps.19.7-Ps.19.14; this torah panel and the heavens panel that precedes it remain one composition's two internal movements, not separate parents.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: The title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David” (web:Ps.19.0) opens a psalm whose two halves name God differently. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (web:Ps.19.1) renders אֵ֑ל, El (oshb:Ps.19.2) — the pointed divine name, distinct from the negative particle אַֽל, 'not,' that appears later in this psalm at oshb:Ps.19.14 — and the covenant name Yahweh does not occur within web:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6 (0 occurrences across 6 verses, confirmed by direct verse-text inspection against the whole-psalm Yahweh count in the device inventory, not a sweep.py lexeme-index feature). This heavens-panel describes creation's speechless testimony through the sun's circuit — “There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard” (web:Ps.19.3), “His going out is from the end of the heavens, his circuit to its ends” (web:Ps.19.6) — in third-person cosmic description without addressing God directly; the panel that follows opens by naming Yahweh's law and shifts into the psalmist's own petitionary voice, marking the seam between the psalm's two halves.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Psalm 19 as one undivided strophe would fold this speechless cosmic testimony together with the psalmist's own petitionary voice that opens in the panel that follows.
observed_substrate_signals: אֵ֑ל (El, oshb:Ps.19.2) is the one divine-name token in web:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6 (sweep: 1 occurrence across 6 verses)

Yahweh (the covenant name) does not appear in web:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6 (0 occurrences across 6 verses, confirmed by direct verse inspection); the psalm's own Yahweh occurrences all fall from web:Ps.19.7 onward
prev_row.device_notes: The composition-level parent is Psalm 19 itself. No selah interrupts web:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The opening strophe is second-person intercession addressed to Yahweh on the king’s behalf, opening “May Yahweh answer you in the day of trouble” (web:Ps.20.1) and running through a chain of jussive petitions (help, support, remembered offerings) that closes on the Selah-marked “remember all your offerings, and accept your burned sacrifice. Selah.” (web:Ps.20.3). The jussive register continues through web:Ps.20.4 (“May he grant you your heart's desire,” יִֽתֶּן, oshb:Ps.20.5), and the verb mood shifts from jussive petition to cohortative communal vow only at this row's own closing verse, “We will triumph in your salvation... we will set up our banners” (web:Ps.20.5, נְרַנְּנָ֤ה/נִדְגֹּ֑ל, oshb:Ps.20.6), which the strophe that follows carries forward as a confident declaration on the king's behalf.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: One whole-psalm row was considered given the psalm’s 9-verse length, but the jussive-petition block (1-5) and the declarative confidence block (6-9, opening “Now I know”, web:Ps.20.6) are distinct enough in mood and person to warrant separate rows.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 1 at Ps.20.1-Ps.20.2, 2 at Ps.20.5 (verse_map_web)
web_selah: true at Ps.20.3 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.20.4 MT)

next_row.device_notes: Psalm 20 holds together as one royal intercession, with its rows gathered under a shared parent. Psalm 20 and Psalm 21 form a royal pair — a pre-battle intercession for the king answered by a psalm of thanksgiving for his victory; two parents, no merged row.

queue_items.claim: The strongest_rejected_alternative's exclusivity claim 'the psalm's one cohortative verb' is byte-false: Psalm 34 carries two he-cohortative forms, and the row's own oss states the correct count object ('the final plural-cohortative verb').
queue_items.grounds: Byte tier over MT 34:2-23: two first-person prefix-conjugation forms carry the cohortative he -- אֲבָרֲכָ֣ה at MT 34:2 (1cs, = web:Ps.34.1) and וּנְרוֹמְמָ֖ה at MT 34:4 (1cp, = web:Ps.34.3); both collate at BYTE tier at their cited refs. No other candidate qualifies (MT 34:9's yechese is a III-he 3ms imperfect; MT 34:21's nishberah is a 3fs Niphal perfect). So 'the psalm's one cohortative verb' fails as written, while the parenthetical 'it occurs exactly once in the psalm' is true only of the token וּנְרוֹמְמָ֖ה. Load-bearing check: the corrected count object does NOT damage the rival's rejection -- both cohortatives stand inside this row's own span web:Ps.34.1-Ps.34.3 and neither recurs from web:Ps.34.4 on, where MT 34:5 opens 1cs testimony -- so the seam and the rejection survive once the object is named. The row contradicts itself between fields, which is what lifts this above a wording nit.
queue_items.proposed_change: Field repair (strongest_rejected_alternative): name the count object as the row's own oss already does -- 'the psalm's one 1cp cohortative, וּנְרוֹמְמָ֖ה (oshb:Ps.34.4 = web:Ps.34.3), stands inside this row's span and no cohortative of either person recurs from web:Ps.34.4 on'. No span change; routes onward as a medium.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: A person shift closes the psalm: נַ֭פְשֵׁנוּ חִכְּתָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.33.20) “Our soul has waited for Yahweh” opens web:Ps.33.20 with נַ֭פְשֵׁנוּ, a noun (“soul”) bearing the first-person-plural possessive suffix (“our”), governing the third-person-feminine-singular verb חִכְּתָ֣ה (“has waited”, agreeing with the feminine noun nefesh); this plural self-reference is not used earlier in the psalm, replacing the third-person “he/his” language of web:Ps.33.13-19 with a congregational “we/our” voice that continues through the closing petition יְהִֽי חַסְדְּךָ֣ יְהוָ֣ה עָלֵ֑ינוּ (oshb:Ps.33.22) “Let your loving kindness be on us, Yahweh” (web:Ps.33.22).
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.33.20-22 as a continuation of the providence unit was rejected: the pronoun shifts from third-person “him/his” description of Yahweh's oversight to a plural “our/we” congregational address, a change in speaker voice the preceding eight verses do not share.

queue_items.claim: observed_substrate_signals[1] labels בַּיהוָ֑ה a vow verb and glosses it 'shall be joyful'; בַּיהוָ֑ה is the preposition-plus-divine-name phrase 'in Yahweh', and the verb carrying that gloss is תָּגִ֣יל.
queue_items.grounds: MT 35:9 reads וְ֭נַפְשִׁי תָּגִ֣יל בַּיהוָ֑ה תָּ֝שִׂישׂ בִּישׁוּעָתֽוֹ (WEB “My soul shall be joyful in Yahweh. It shall rejoice in his salvation.”, web:Ps.35.9; identity psalm). Token order: תָּגִ֣יל is the verb 'shall be joyful', בַּיהוָ֑ה the prepositional phrase 'in Yahweh', תָּ֝שִׂישׂ the second vow verb 'shall rejoice'. The splice is byte-valid (it collates at BYTE tier at oshb:Ps.35.9) but is semantically the wrong word for the claim, and quote/gloss parity fails: a two-item list of 'vow verbs' pairs one real verb with a prepositional phrase. The row's own boundary_rationale gets it right, splicing the verse's opening run and glossing it as the vow, so the row contradicts itself between fields. The seam is unaffected -- the mood does turn from imprecation to vow at web:Ps.35.9, and the row's other substrate signal (the imperative cluster at MT 35:1-3, all three splices byte-collated) is true -- so the defect is a defective recorded warrant, not a boundary error.
queue_items.proposed_change: Field repair (observed_substrate_signals[1]): 'the vow verbs תָּגִ֣יל and תָּ֝שִׂישׂ (oshb:Ps.35.9) replace the imprecative mood of web:Ps.35.4-Ps.35.8'. No span change; routes onward as a medium.

trigger_dispositions.grounds: The matched phrase 'this cycle' in strongest_rejected_alternative ('it reads as this cycle's close rather than a fresh movement') denotes a literary unit of Psalm 35 -- the petition-to-vow cycle -- not a session, wave or authoring pass; the retro-scan match is a false positive of the session/wave class. TEST 1: the prose describes the text, not the process. TEST 2 arm: the cross-unit claim it carries is verse-anchored as sec.10 requires and re-derives TRUE -- the three vow returns stand at MT 35:9 (וְ֭נַפְשִׁי תָּגִ֣יל בַּיהוָ֑ה תָּ֝שִׂישׂ בִּישׁוּעָתֽוֹ; WEB “My soul shall be joyful in Yahweh. It shall rejoice in his salvation.”, web:Ps.35.9), MT 35:18 and MT 35:27-28 in an identity psalm needing no dual-cite, and the row cites them as web:Ps.35.18 and web:Ps.35.27-Ps.35.28. No register violation on this tag.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: The unit opens on direct imperative address to Yahweh, רִיבָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה אֶת יְרִיבַ֑י (oshb:Ps.35.1) “Contend, Yahweh, with those who contend with me.” (web:Ps.35.1), and runs an imprecation against the psalmist’s pursuers through web:Ps.35.8; it turns at web:Ps.35.9-Ps.35.10 into a vow spoken in the psalmist’s own voice, וְ֭נַפְשִׁי תָּגִ֣יל (oshb:Ps.35.9) “My soul shall be joyful in Yahweh.” (web:Ps.35.9), a petition-to-vow turn that recurs as the close of this psalm’s two later complaint cycles (web:Ps.35.18, web:Ps.35.27-Ps.35.28).

shipped_row.device_notes: All of Psalm 35's rows meet in one parent. The psalm runs three petition-to-vow cycles closing at web:Ps.35.9-Ps.35.10, web:Ps.35.18, and web:Ps.35.27-Ps.35.28; this row covers the opening cycle.

observed_substrate_signals: the span runs ayin through tav (web:Ps.34.15-21) in unbroken acrostic sequence, then closes on a פ verse one position beyond the standard 22-letter/22-verse acrostic run
פּוֹדֶ֣ה יְ֭הוָה נֶ֣פֶשׁ עֲבָדָ֑יו (oshb:Ps.34.23) opens with פ, the acrostic's trailing extra letter per psalm_device_inventory.json

queue_items.claim: boundary_rationale says the plural 'the wicked' opens the span's first verse while citing the Hebrew token at oshb:Ps.37.20, but MT 37:20 opens on the kaf particle — the row's own acrostic warrant — with that plural standing second.
queue_items.grounds: MT 37:20 reads כִּ֤י, then רְשָׁעִ֨ים (both collated byte at oshb:Ps.37.20; word order taken from verse_map_oshb.json). The row asserts the opposite twice elsewhere — observed_substrate_signals ('surface כ at web:Ps.37.20 sits on the causal particle') and device_notes ('The surface letter at web:Ps.37.20 sits on the causal particle ... rather than a fresh content word') — so the claim contradicts the row's own driver in a psalm whose entire method is which word opens a verse. The position holds only of the WEB rendering ('But the wicked shall perish.'), i.e. a WEB word-order fact attached to an oshb-cited token.
queue_items.proposed_change: Field repair, boundary_rationale, no span effect: '...and the related plural (oshb:Ps.37.20) stands as the second word of the span's first verse, web:Ps.37.20, immediately after the kaf particle' — or simply 'occurs in' for 'opens'.

trigger_dispositions.grounds: Calibration holds; medium_low is honest and, if anything, conservative. Both seams stand at structural acrostic positions re-derived from bytes: kaf opens the row's first verse MT 37:20 on the particle כִּ֤י (collated byte at oshb:Ps.37.20) and nun opens MT 37:25 immediately past the row's close, so the outer bounds coincide with the complete letter groups kaf (37:20), lamed (37:21-22) and mem (37:23-24). The stated reason for the low band is byte-true: lamed לֹוֶ֣ה opens MT 37:21 one verse after kaf — one of the psalm's five length-irregularities (dalet, kaf and qof 1 verse; samekh 3; shin 4) — and the kaf position sits on a particle rather than a content word, precisely the surface/buried-letter caveat Ps strategy §2e requires for Ps 37. No cap applies (a strophe row inside a long psalm; the whole_psalm ruling is not in play) and no frontier flag is warranted. shipped_row.boundary_rationale: The historical address opens on the wilderness march, “God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness” (web:Ps.68.7), closed by a Selah, and continues through Sinai theophany imagery, “The earth trembled. The sky also poured down rain at the presence of the God of Sinai” (web:Ps.68.8), into a battle report whose vocabulary is genuinely obscure: “She who waits at home divides the plunder” (web:Ps.68.12), “the wings of a dove sheathed with silver, her feathers with shining gold” (web:Ps.68.13), plus “it snowed on Zalmon” (web:Ps.68.14). The strophe is bounded by the vocative-plus-Selah opening at web:Ps.68.7 and the scene shift to direct address of the Bashan mountains at web:Ps.68.15; its interior (web:Ps.68.9-web:Ps.68.14) resists a finer tier-1 split — the identity of the home-waiting figure and the referent of the silver-dove and Zalmon-snow images are argued in the commentary tradition, not settled by the bytes available here.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: Psalm 68 opens on a 3rd-person jussive triad, “Let God arise! Let his enemies be scattered! Let them who hate him also flee before him.” (web:Ps.68.1), followed by the psalm's genuine imperative opener, a four-verb summons, “Sing to God! Sing praises to his name! Extol him who rides on the clouds: to Yah, his name! Rejoice before him!” (web:Ps.68.4). The strophe closes on a verbless construct-noun clause, “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.” (web:Ps.68.5), then the strophe's genuine participles, “God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing” (web:Ps.68.6); the shift from imperative summons to this closing description marks this strophe's own close before the historical address opens at web:Ps.68.7.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.68.7 to fold in the wilderness-march recollection was rejected: web:Ps.68.7 opens with direct vocative address, “God, when you went out before your people,” a historical-narrative register distinct from the character description of web:Ps.68.5-web:Ps.68.6.
observed_substrate_signals: A 3rd-person jussive triad (“Let… Let… Let…”) opens the psalm (web:Ps.68.1); its verbs are prefix-conjugation forms with expressed subjects, not imperatives.
The psalm's actual imperative opener is a four-verb cluster, “Sing to God! Sing praises…” (web:Ps.68.4), distinct in form from the jussive triad of web:Ps.68.1.

web:Ps.68.5 (“is God in his holy habitation”) is a verbless construct-noun clause, not participial; the strophe's genuine participles open the next verse instead, “God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing” (web:Ps.68.6), replacing the imperative mood running through web:Ps.68.1 (3rd-person jussive) and web:Ps.68.4 (true imperative).

next_row.boundary_rationale: A verbless anaphoric description turns to the rival mountain, “The mountains of Bashan are majestic mountains. The mountains of Bashan are rugged.” (web:Ps.68.15), before direct second-person address opens with an envy motif, “Why do you look in envy, you rugged mountains, at the mountain where God chooses to reign?” (web:Ps.68.16). The scene then follows the procession itself: “The chariots of God are tens of thousands and thousands of thousands.” (web:Ps.68.17), tracked “from Sinai, into the sanctuary” (web:Ps.68.17), and “You have ascended on high. You have led away captives.” (web:Ps.68.18). web:Ps.68.15's anaphoric mountain description is a verbless 3rd-person noun chain; the tier-1 vocative-shift opener is the direct address beginning at web:Ps.68.16 (“you rugged mountains”); the chariot count and the referent of “ascended on high” (web:Ps.68.18) are debated across the commentary tradition, holding this strophe at reduced confidence relative to its clearer opening.
